b. 
```{r, echo=TRUE}
library(igraph)
#A : Plot Degree Distribution
hist(igraph::degree(dolphins), xlab = "Vertex Degree", 
     ylab = "Frequency", main = "Dolphins")
#B: Density
edge_density(dolphins)
#C : Clustering
transitivity(dolphins, "global")
#D: Centrality
cent_table<- data.frame(
closeness = igraph::closeness(dolphins),
harmonic = harmonic_centrality(dolphins, normalized = TRUE),
betweeness = igraph::betweenness(dolphins, normalized = TRUE),
eigenvector = eigen_centrality(dolphins)$vector,
pagerank = page_rank(dolphins)$vector
)
head(cent_table, n=10)
#Mean centrality across nodes
colMeans(cent_table)

#E: Assortativity
assortativity_degree(dolphins)
#F: Community Detection
plot(cluster_fast_greedy(dolphins), dolphins)
```
By the histogram we plotted, it seems that the degree distribution of the dolphins graph is fairly evenly distributed with some minor skewness to the right. We also see that the edge density is only 0.08 providing for a less dense network. Looking at the aggregated centrality, it seems like the network as a whole has substantially low closeness centrality with only 0.005 but quite high harmonic centrality with 0.379.There also seems to be negative assortativity in the network and 4 detected networks via fast and greedy. 




c. 
```{r, echo=TRUE}

#Size of node correlates with degree
V(dolphins)$size <- 1.5*(igraph::degree(dolphins))
plot(dolphins, vertex.label = NA, layout = layout.circle)

# Node color represented by Betweenness quantiles 
b <- igraph::betweenness(dolphins, normalized = TRUE)
V(dolphins)$color <- ifelse(b < quantile(b, 0.25), "red", 
                            ifelse(b < quantile(b, 0.5), "blue",
                                   ifelse(b < quantile(b, 0.75),
                                          "green", "orange")))
plot(dolphins, vertex.label = NA, layout = layout_as_tree)

# Shape of nodes represented by eigenvector centrality quantiles
e <- eigen_centrality(dolphins)$vector
plot(dolphins, vertex.label = NA, vertex.shape = ifelse(e<quantile(e,0.25), 
                  "square", ifelse(e < quantile(e, 0.5), "circle", 
                    ifelse(e < quantile(e, 0.75), "sphere", "crectangle"))),
                   layout = layout_components)
```
Of these 3 graphs I belueve the tree layout represents the network the best. Also, with full disclosure I believe the different shapes of the nodes make the graph more confusing, so I believe the optimal graph for this network would be the second one when taking visualization into account.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Simulation (Classical)
set.seed(1000)
dolphinsg <- vector('list', 1000)
for(i in 1:1000){
        dolphinsg[[i]] <- erdos.renyi.game(n = gorder(dolphins), 
                                           p.or.m = edge_density(dolphins),
                                           type = "gnp")
}

# Average Degree
avgdegree <- rep(mean(degree(dolphins)),1000)
#Observed Value 
avgdegree[1]
#Simulation
avgdegreesim <- unlist(sapply(dolphinsg, function(x) mean(degree(x))))
# P Value
mean(avgdegree>avgdegreesim)

# Centrality Measures

#Observed Value 
closeness[1]
#Simulation

closenesssim[is.na(closenesssim)]<- 0
# P Value
mean(closeness>closenesssim)
```

When observing the classical vs. the generalized random graph simulation, the first aspect I notice is that there are more significant results among the generalized random graph than the classical Erdos Renyi random graph for a given characteristic. Another complication worth mentioning is that the generalized random graph models did not work for simulating community detection via fast and greedy. This is why I commented it out at the end with the Error message included. 




e. 
```{r, echo=TRUE}
#Call sand package
library(sand)

#### Induced Subgraph Sampling ####
g1 <- igraph::induced_subgraph(dolphins, sample(seq_len(vcount(dolphins)) ,
                                                size = 30))
plot(g1, layout=layout.fruchterman.reingold,edge.arrow.size=.1, vertex.size=2)
mean(degree(g1))
edge_density(g1)
transitivity(g1, type=c("global"))
eigen_centrality(g1)$vector
assortativity_degree(g1)

#### Incident Subgraph Sampling ####
g2 <- igraph::subgraph.edges(dolphins, sample(seq_len(ecount(dolphins)) ,
                                              size = 80))
plot(g2, layout=layout.fruchterman.reingold, edge.arrow.size=.1, vertex.size=1)
mean(degree(g2))
edge_density(g2)
transitivity(g2, type=c("global"))
eigen_centrality(g2)$vector
assortativity_degree(g2)


#### Snowball Sampling  #### 
n_seeds=5
g3 <- graph.neighborhood(dolphins, order=1, 
      nodes=sample(seq_len(vcount(dolphins)) ,size = n_seeds), mode=c("all"))
g3 <- graph.disjoint.union(g3)

mean(degree(g3))
mean(betweenness(g3))
transitivity(g3, type=c("global"))
eigen_centrality(g3)$vector
assortativity_degree(g3)
```
From Induced Subgraph sampling to Incident subgraph sampling, we see that mean degree, edge density, and assortativity stay about the same, yet global transitivity splits in half from 0.3962 to 0.1682. More apparent is the drastic increase in eigenvector centrality in this same comparison.  As for snowball sampling, using the same values in the sample code, we see a drastic increase across all measures except transitivity which stays at about $0.125$. There is also negative assortativity which represents the true network better than the other sampling methods.

I chose to re-do the erdos renyi and vary the sampling probabilities by cutting the edge density in half from $0.084$ to  $0.042$. I will now review the plots I made for the mean of each characteristic against the network size vector. First, the Average degree seems to have an exactly linear relationship with the size of the network. This intuitively makes sense because the nodes are staying relatively constant while network size varies, especially in this formulation of the network. Average Closeness centrality seems to have a very slight positive relationship with network size. Average Harmonic Centrality has a stronger positive linear relationship with Network Size, Average Betweenness Centrality has a slight negative relationship with network size, Average Eigenvector Centrality seems to have a slight positive relationship with Network Size, Average Page Rank Centrality stays constant with Network Size, Average Assortativity stays approximately constant, Average Transitivity by Network Size seems to have an approximately constant relationship with Network Size, while it also has an interesting pattern where there are multiple strong relationshiips and a good amount of observations with average transitivity 0. Average Edge Density by Network Size seems to have a constant linear relationship with Network Size, The average number of communities seem to have a negative relationship with Network Size with very little overlapping points.
